stem: In supervised training, what is the loss function used for?
explanation: The loss turns the gap between predictions and targets into one number; training adjusts the parameters to make it small. It does not choose the architecture or split the data.

options.label: A
options.text: To decide how many layers the model needs

options.label: B
options.text: To measure how wrong the model's predictions are, so the optimiser can reduce that number

options.label: C
options.text: To split the data into training and validation sets

options.label: D
options.text: To convert raw inputs into embeddings

stem: Which loss is the standard choice for multi-class classification?
explanation: Cross-entropy (log loss) compares predicted class probabilities with the true class and gives smooth, strong gradients. Accuracy is a metric, not a trainable loss, and MSE/MAE are meant for numeric targets.

options.label: A
options.text: Mean squared error

options.label: B
options.text: Mean absolute error

options.label: C
options.text: Accuracy

options.label: D
options.text: Cross-entropy

stem: Targets are [3, 5, 2] and predictions are [2.5, 5, 4]. What is the mean squared error?
explanation: The errors are 0.5, 0 and -2; their squares are 0.25, 0 and 4, which sum to 4.25. Dividing by 3 gives about 1.417. 0.833 is the MAE, and 4.25 forgets to take the mean.

options.label: A
options.text: About 1.417

options.label: B
options.text: About 0.833

stem: A classifier assigns probability 0.1 to the correct class. What is its cross-entropy loss (natural log)?
explanation: Cross-entropy is -ln(p_true) = -ln(0.1) ≈ 2.303. The value 0.105 is -ln(0.9), which would be the loss if the model had given the correct class 0.9.

options.label: C
options.text: About 2.303

options.label: D
options.text: About 0.105

stem: Why is accuracy usually not used directly as the training loss?
explanation: Accuracy only changes when a prediction crosses the decision threshold, so small parameter changes usually leave it unchanged and its gradient is zero. Cross-entropy changes smoothly as probabilities move, so it always shows a direction to improve.

options.label: A
options.text: It is too expensive to compute on large batches

options.label: B
options.text: It is flat almost everywhere, so it gives the optimiser no gradient signal

options.label: C
options.text: It can only be used for regression problems

options.label: D
options.text: It always overestimates how well the model performs

stem: Compared with mean absolute error (MAE), mean squared error (MSE)...
explanation: Squaring makes an error of 10 cost 100 while an error of 2 costs 4, so a few large errors dominate MSE. MAE grows linearly and is more robust. Neither loss can be negative.

options.label: A
options.text: penalises large errors much more heavily, so it is more sensitive to outliers

options.label: B
options.text: treats all errors the same regardless of their size

options.label: C
options.text: can become negative when predictions are too high

options.label: D
options.text: is only defined for classification problems

stem: An untrained 10-class classifier outputs uniform probabilities. Roughly what cross-entropy loss should it start with?
explanation: Uniform probabilities give the correct class p = 1/10, so the loss is -ln(0.1) = ln 10 ≈ 2.303. This makes a useful sanity check: a starting loss far above ln C suggests a bug.

options.label: D
options.text: About 2.303

stem: An input has several plausible targets. Minimising mean squared error drives the model to predict which summary of them?
explanation: The value that minimises the average squared error is the mean. Minimising absolute error instead gives the median, which is why MAE is more robust to outliers.

options.label: A
options.text: The median

options.label: B
options.text: The most frequent value

options.label: C
options.text: The mean

options.label: D
options.text: The largest value

stem: Explain why cross-entropy is preferred over accuracy as the training loss for a classifier.
explanation: Accuracy has no useful gradient; cross-entropy is smooth and punishes confident mistakes.

criteria.description: States that accuracy is flat or piecewise constant, so it gives (almost) no gradient for the optimiser
States that cross-entropy is smooth/differentiable and changes as the predicted probabilities change
Mentions that cross-entropy strongly penalises confident wrong predictions (loss grows as -ln p)

rubric.modelAnswer: Accuracy only changes when a prediction crosses the decision threshold, so for small weight changes it stays the same and its gradient is zero almost everywhere; gradient descent gets no signal. Cross-entropy, -ln(p of the true class), changes smoothly whenever probabilities shift, so there is always a direction to improve, and it punishes confident wrong answers heavily because the loss grows without bound as that probability approaches zero.

stem: In the update θ ← θ − η∇L(θ), what does η control?
explanation: η is the learning rate: it scales the gradient to decide how far each update moves the parameters. Batch size and regularisation strength are separate hyperparameters.

options.label: A
options.text: The number of layers in the model

options.label: B
options.text: The batch size

options.label: C
options.text: The size of each step (the learning rate)

options.label: D
options.text: The strength of regularisation

stem: Why does gradient descent subtract the gradient rather than add it?
explanation: The gradient points uphill. Stepping against it moves downhill on the loss surface. Adding it would make the loss rise.

options.label: A
options.text: The gradient points in the direction of steepest increase, so moving the opposite way decreases the loss

options.label: B
options.text: Subtraction is cheaper than addition on GPUs

options.label: C
options.text: The gradient is always negative

options.label: D
options.text: To keep all weights positive

stem: For L(w) = (w − 3)², starting at w = 0 with learning rate 0.1, what is w after one gradient descent step?
explanation: The gradient is 2(w − 3) = −6 at w = 0. The update is w = 0 − 0.1 × (−6) = 0.6. Getting −0.6 means the gradient was added instead of subtracted.

stem: Your training loss rises every step and soon becomes NaN. What is the most sensible first fix?
explanation: A loss that grows and then becomes NaN is the classic sign of steps that overshoot and diverge. Reducing the learning rate (often by 3–10×) is the first thing to try.

options.label: A
options.text: Increase the learning rate

options.label: B
options.text: Add more layers

options.label: C
options.text: Delete the validation set

options.label: D
options.text: Reduce the learning rate

stem: What is mini-batch gradient descent?
explanation: Mini-batch gradient descent averages the gradient over a small random batch (for example 32–1024 examples). It is far cheaper than full-batch descent, and its noise can even help generalisation.

options.label: A
options.text: Using the whole training set to compute every step

options.label: B
options.text: Estimating the gradient from a small random subset of examples at each step

options.label: C
options.text: Updating one parameter at a time

options.label: D
options.text: Training only the last layer of a network

stem: What is one epoch?
explanation: An epoch is one pass over every training example. With 50,000 examples and batch size 128, one epoch is 391 steps.

options.label: A
options.text: A single optimiser step

options.label: B
options.text: A single mini-batch

options.label: C
options.text: One full pass over the training data

options.label: D
options.text: The time until the loss stops improving

stem: For L(w) = (w − 3)², which learning rate makes gradient descent diverge?
explanation: Each step multiplies the distance to the minimum by (1 − 2η). For η = 1.1 that factor is −1.2, so the distance grows every step. η = 0.9 gives −0.8, which oscillates but still converges; η = 0.5 jumps straight to the minimum.

stem: What does the Adam optimiser add compared with plain SGD?
explanation: Adam keeps a momentum-like average m of gradients and an average v of squared gradients and steps by roughly η·m/√v. It still needs a learning rate and does not guarantee a global minimum.

options.label: A
options.text: It computes exact second derivatives (the Hessian) at every step

options.label: B
options.text: It guarantees finding the global minimum

options.label: C
options.text: It removes the need for a learning rate

options.label: D
options.text: Running averages of the gradients (momentum) and of squared gradients, giving each parameter its own effective step size

stem: For L(w) = (w − 3)², start at w = 0 with learning rate 0.1. Compute w after one gradient descent step and explain each part of the update.
explanation: Gradient −6, new w = 0.6; subtracting the gradient moves downhill, scaled by the learning rate.

criteria.description: Computes the gradient correctly: dL/dw = 2(w − 3) = −6 at w = 0
Gets the new value w = 0.6 with the correct sign (subtracting η times the gradient)
Explains that the gradient points uphill so we step against it, and the learning rate sets the step size

rubric.modelAnswer: The derivative is dL/dw = 2(w − 3), which is −6 at w = 0. The update is w ← w − η·gradient = 0 − 0.1 × (−6) = 0.6. We subtract because the gradient points in the direction of steepest increase, so stepping against it lowers the loss; the learning rate 0.1 scales how far we move. The loss drops from 9 to 5.76.

stem: Training loss keeps falling while validation loss starts to rise. This is a sign of:
explanation: A widening gap, with training loss still improving and validation loss getting worse, means the model is memorising training data rather than learning patterns that generalise.

options.label: A
options.text: Overfitting

options.label: B
options.text: Underfitting

options.label: C
options.text: A learning rate that is too small

options.label: D
options.text: A perfectly tuned model

stem: What is the validation set used for?
explanation: The validation set guides decisions such as λ, learning rate and early stopping. The test set, not the validation set, is the one you touch once at the end.

options.label: A
options.text: Computing the gradients for each update

options.label: B
options.text: Reporting one final, untouched number at the end of the project

options.label: C
options.text: Choosing hyperparameters and deciding when to stop training

options.label: D
options.text: Generating augmented training examples

stem: With weights w = [3, −1, 0.5] and λ = 0.1, what is the L2 penalty λ·Σw²?
explanation: Σw² = 9 + 1 + 0.25 = 10.25, and 0.1 × 10.25 = 1.025. The value 0.45 is the L1 penalty (0.1 × (3 + 1 + 0.5)); 10.25 forgets to multiply by λ.

stem: Why does L1 regularisation tend to produce weights that are exactly zero?
explanation: The L1 gradient is λ·sign(w), the same size for tiny and large weights, so small weights get pushed all the way to zero. L2's push (2λw) shrinks as the weight shrinks, so weights get small but rarely exactly zero. Randomly zeroing units is dropout.

options.label: A
options.text: It squares the weights, so small ones become negligible

options.label: B
options.text: Its gradient is a constant-size push towards zero regardless of a weight's magnitude, so small weights reach exactly zero

options.label: C
options.text: It only applies to bias terms

options.label: D
options.text: It randomly sets weights to zero at each step

stem: What does dropout do during training?
explanation: Dropout zeroes random activations each step, so the network cannot rely on any single unit. Stopping on validation loss is early stopping, a different technique.

options.label: A
options.text: Removes difficult examples from the training set

options.label: B
options.text: Randomly sets hidden activations to zero with probability p

options.label: C
options.text: Stops training when validation loss stops improving

options.label: D
options.text: Halves the learning rate every epoch

stem: Training loss is 0.85 and validation loss is 0.88, both well above what similar models achieve. What is the best next step?
explanation: Both losses are high and close together, which indicates underfitting (high bias). More regularisation would make it worse; the model needs more capacity or more training.

options.label: A
options.text: Increase model capacity or train longer, because the model is underfitting

options.label: B
options.text: Add much stronger regularisation

options.label: C
options.text: Remove half of the training data

options.label: D
options.text: Use early stopping, because the model is overfitting

stem: You normalise features using the mean and standard deviation of the entire dataset, then split it into train and validation sets. What is the problem?
explanation: This is data leakage: the training pipeline has seen information from the validation data. Compute normalisation statistics on the training split only, then apply them to the other splits.

options.label: A
options.text: There is no problem; normalisation is unrelated to splitting

options.label: B
options.text: It only makes training slower

options.label: C
options.text: Validation statistics leak into training, so validation scores become optimistic

options.label: D
options.text: It forces the model to underfit

stem: With inverted dropout and p = 0.5, what happens to the surviving activations during training, and what happens at inference?
explanation: Inverted dropout scales kept activations by 1/(1 − p) = 2 so their expected value is unchanged, which lets inference run with dropout switched off and no rescaling. Leaving dropout on at inference makes predictions random.

options.label: A
options.text: They are multiplied by 0.5 during training, and dropout stays on at inference

options.label: B
options.text: They are left unchanged, and half the units are still dropped at inference

options.label: C
options.text: They are multiplied by 2 during training, and dropout stays on at inference

options.label: D
options.text: They are multiplied by 2 during training, and dropout is switched off at inference

stem: Training loss falls steadily, but validation loss has started rising. Diagnose the problem and suggest two remedies.
explanation: Overfitting; remedies include early stopping, weight decay, dropout, more data or a smaller model.

criteria.description: Identifies overfitting (the model memorises training data and fails to generalise)
Gives at least two valid remedies, e.g. early stopping, L2/weight decay, dropout, more or augmented data, a smaller model (1 point each, max 2)

rubric.modelAnswer: This is overfitting: the model keeps fitting the training data, including its noise, while performance on unseen data gets worse. Remedies: use early stopping and keep the weights from the best validation point; add L2 regularisation (weight decay) or dropout; collect more data or use data augmentation; or reduce model capacity.

stem: Why do neural networks need non-linear activation functions?
explanation: W₂(W₁x) = (W₂W₁)x, so purely linear layers add no expressive power. A non-linearity between layers lets the network model curved functions and decision boundaries.

options.label: A
options.text: To make matrix multiplication faster

options.label: B
options.text: Without them, any stack of linear layers collapses into a single linear transformation

options.label: C
options.text: To keep all weights positive

options.label: D
options.text: To normalise the inputs

stem: What is ReLU(−2)?
explanation: ReLU(z) = max(0, z), so any negative input becomes 0. The value 0.12 is roughly sigmoid(−2), a different activation.

stem: What is the maximum value of the derivative of the sigmoid function?
explanation: σ'(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)), which is largest when σ(z) = 0.5, giving 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25. The value 0.5 is σ(0) itself, not its derivative. This small maximum is why deep sigmoid networks suffer from vanishing gradients.

stem: A neuron has x = [1, 2], w = [0.5, −0.25] and b = 0.1. What are its pre-activation z and its ReLU output?
explanation: z = 0.5×1 + (−0.25)×2 + 0.1 = 0.5 − 0.5 + 0.1 = 0.1. Since z > 0, ReLU passes it through unchanged: 0.1.

options.label: A
options.text: z = 0.1 and ReLU(z) = 0.1

options.label: B
options.text: z = 0.1 and ReLU(z) = 0

options.label: C
options.text: z = −0.1 and ReLU(z) = 0

options.label: D
options.text: z = 1.1 and ReLU(z) = 1.1

stem: Which activation is the usual choice for the output of a binary classifier?
explanation: Sigmoid maps any score to (0, 1), which can be read as the probability of the positive class and pairs naturally with binary cross-entropy. ReLU outputs are unbounded and not probabilities.

options.label: A
options.text: ReLU

options.label: B
options.text: Tanh

options.label: C
options.text: Sigmoid

options.label: D
options.text: No activation at all

stem: What is a 'dead ReLU'?
explanation: When z < 0 for all inputs, ReLU's derivative is 0 everywhere, so no gradient reaches the neuron's weights and it stays off permanently. Leaky ReLU avoids this with a small negative slope.

options.label: A
options.text: A neuron whose output is always exactly 1

options.label: B
options.text: A neuron whose pre-activation is negative for every input, so its gradient is always zero and it never updates

options.label: C
options.text: A ReLU that has been replaced by GELU

options.label: D
options.text: A neuron temporarily removed by dropout

stem: Through 10 sigmoid layers, even in the best case, the gradient reaching the first layer is scaled by roughly:
explanation: Each sigmoid layer multiplies the gradient by at most 0.25, so ten layers give 0.25¹⁰ = 1/1,048,576 ≈ 9.5 × 10⁻⁷. This is the vanishing-gradient problem that ReLU-family activations largely solve.

stem: You apply softmax to your model's outputs and then pass them to PyTorch's CrossEntropyLoss. What happens?
explanation: CrossEntropyLoss applies log-softmax internally and expects logits. Passing probabilities squashes them again, flattening the distribution and weakening gradients, with no error to warn you.

options.label: A
options.text: Softmax is effectively applied twice, because the loss expects raw logits; training still runs but is weakened

options.label: B
options.text: Nothing; this is the recommended usage

options.label: C
options.text: The loss becomes negative

options.label: D
options.text: PyTorch raises an error

stem: Why does a deep network need non-linear activation functions? Give a short mathematical argument.
explanation: Linear layers compose into one linear layer; non-linearities let depth add expressive power.

criteria.description: Shows or states that stacked linear layers collapse to one linear map, e.g. W₂(W₁x) = (W₂W₁)x
Explains that non-linearities let the network represent curved functions / non-linear decision boundaries, so depth adds power

rubric.modelAnswer: Without activations, two layers compute y = W₂(W₁x) = (W₂W₁)x = Wx, which is just one linear layer; any number of linear layers collapses the same way and can only draw straight (linear) decision boundaries. Putting a non-linearity such as ReLU between layers breaks this collapse, so each layer can bend the representation and the network can approximate complex, non-linear functions.

stem: Which statement about the chain rule in backpropagation is correct?
explanation: Backpropagation moves from the output backward. Each layer takes the gradient arriving from above and multiplies it by its own local derivative.

options.label: A
options.text: Gradients are computed from the input forward

options.label: B
options.text: Each layer multiplies the incoming gradient by its local derivative

options.label: C
options.text: Weights are updated before gradients exist

options.label: D
options.text: Only the final layer receives a gradient

stem: In which direction do gradients flow during backpropagation?
explanation: Values flow forward during the forward pass; gradients flow backward, starting from the loss (where ∂L/∂L = 1) and moving towards the input.

options.label: A
options.text: From the loss at the output back towards the input

options.label: B
options.text: From the input forward to the output

options.label: C
options.text: In a random order chosen each step

options.label: D
options.text: Only within the output layer

stem: What is the difference between backpropagation and gradient descent?
explanation: Backpropagation is the method for computing ∂L/∂θ efficiently. An optimiser such as SGD or Adam then uses those gradients to change the weights. Option B has the roles reversed.

options.label: A
options.text: They are two names for the same algorithm

options.label: B
options.text: Backpropagation updates the weights; gradient descent computes the gradients

options.label: C
options.text: Backpropagation computes the gradients; gradient descent (the optimiser) uses them to update the weights

options.label: D
options.text: Backpropagation is only used for convolutional networks

stem: A network computes z = w₁x, h = ReLU(z), ŷ = w₂h and L = (ŷ − y)². With x = 2, y = 1, w₁ = 0.5 and w₂ = 3, what is ∂L/∂w₂?
explanation: Forward: z = 1, h = 1, ŷ = 3, L = 4. Backward: ∂L/∂ŷ = 2(ŷ − y) = 4, and the local derivative of ŷ with respect to w₂ is h = 1, so ∂L/∂w₂ = 4 × 1 = 4. The value 12 is ∂L/∂h.

stem: Same network: z = w₁x, h = ReLU(z), ŷ = w₂h, L = (ŷ − y)², with x = 2, y = 1, w₁ = 0.5, w₂ = 3. What is ∂L/∂w₁?
explanation: ∂L/∂ŷ = 4; times w₂ = 3 gives ∂L/∂h = 12; ReLU's local derivative is 1 since z > 0, so ∂L/∂z = 12; times x = 2 gives ∂L/∂w₁ = 24. Stopping at 12 forgets the last local derivative.

stem: A value feeds into two different later nodes. During the backward pass, how are the gradients from the two paths combined?
explanation: By the multivariable chain rule, the total gradient is the sum of the contributions along every path. That is why frameworks accumulate gradients.

options.label: A
options.text: They are added

options.label: B
options.text: They are multiplied

options.label: C
options.text: Only the larger one is kept

options.label: D
options.text: Only the first path is used

stem: Why do frameworks keep the forward-pass activations in memory during training?
explanation: Local derivatives depend on forward values, e.g. ∂(w·h)/∂w = h. Caching them avoids recomputation and is why training uses much more memory than inference.

options.label: A
options.text: Only for logging and visualisation

options.label: B
options.text: The backward pass needs them to compute local derivatives

options.label: C
options.text: To speed up inference later

options.label: D
options.text: Because dropout requires it

stem: After loss.backward(), a parameter's .grad is None. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Autograd only fills .grad for parameters that require gradients and contributed to the loss. An inactive ReLU gives a gradient of 0, not None; exploding gradients show up as huge or NaN values.

options.label: A
options.text: The learning rate is too high

options.label: B
options.text: A ReLU in front of it was inactive, so its gradient is exactly zero

options.label: C
options.text: Its gradient exploded

options.label: D
options.text: The parameter is not on the computation path to the loss (or does not require gradients)

stem: Describe what happens during the backward pass of backpropagation and why it is efficient.
explanation: Start at the loss, move backward, multiply incoming gradient by each local derivative, reuse results.

criteria.description: States that the backward pass starts at the loss and moves from the output backward towards the input
Explains that each layer/node multiplies the incoming (upstream) gradient by its own local derivative (the chain rule)
Explains efficiency: upstream gradients and cached forward values are reused, so all gradients cost about one extra pass rather than one pass per parameter

rubric.modelAnswer: After the forward pass caches intermediate values, the backward pass starts at the loss with gradient 1 and moves from the output backward. Each layer takes the gradient arriving from above, multiplies it by its own local derivative (chain rule), and passes the result to the layer before it; where a value fans out, gradients are summed. It is efficient because each layer's gradient is built from the one above it and from cached activations, so computing every parameter's gradient costs roughly one extra pass through the network instead of one forward pass per parameter.

stem: What is the main advantage of embeddings over one-hot vectors?
explanation: One-hot vectors make every pair of tokens equally different. Embeddings are learned so similar items get similar vectors, turning similarity into geometry.

options.label: A
options.text: They are longer, so they hold more information

options.label: B
options.text: They are sparse, so they use less memory per token

options.label: C
options.text: They are dense learned vectors in which related items end up close together

options.label: D
options.text: They do not need any training

stem: How is an embedding layer typically implemented?
explanation: An embedding layer is a trainable matrix; token i is represented by row i. The lookup is equivalent to multiplying a one-hot vector by the matrix, but much cheaper.

options.label: A
options.text: As a lookup table: a V × d matrix with one row per token

options.label: B
options.text: As a cryptographic hash of the token text

options.label: C
options.text: As a sorting step over the vocabulary

options.label: D
options.text: As a convolution over characters

stem: What is the cosine similarity of the vectors [1, 0] and [1, 1]?
explanation: The dot product is 1, and the lengths are 1 and √2, so cosine = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707. The vectors are 45° apart, so they are related but not identical.

options.label: B
options.text: About 0.707

stem: If all embeddings are normalised to unit length, which statement is true?
explanation: With ‖a‖ = ‖b‖ = 1, cos(a, b) = a·b, and ‖a − b‖² = 2 − 2cos(a, b), so all three measures agree on ranking. Systems normalise once and then use the cheap dot product.

options.label: A
options.text: Cosine similarity and dot product give different rankings

options.label: B
options.text: Euclidean distance becomes meaningless

options.label: C
options.text: Every dot product equals 1

options.label: D
options.text: The dot product equals cosine similarity, so it ranks results identically

stem: You switched to a new embedding model for new documents but kept the old model's vectors for existing documents. What happens?
explanation: Each model defines its own vector space. Comparing a query from one model with documents from another produces arbitrary scores, often with no error. Re-embed everything when you change models.

options.label: A
options.text: Nothing; all embedding vectors are compatible

options.label: B
options.text: Old documents are found faster than new ones

options.label: C
options.text: Similarity between vectors from different models is meaningless, so search quality silently degrades

options.label: D
options.text: The database rejects vectors from the second model

stem: An embedding table has a vocabulary of 50,000 tokens and dimension 768. How many parameters does it hold?
explanation: One row of 768 numbers per token: 50,000 × 768 = 38,400,000. Adding the two numbers (50,768) is a common slip.

stem: Let a = [1, 2, 2] and c = [2, 4, 4]. Which statement is correct?
explanation: c = 2a, so the angle between them is zero and cosine = 18/(3 × 6) = 1. Euclidean distance still sees the length difference: ‖a − c‖ = ‖[−1, −2, −2]‖ = 3. The dot product is 18.

options.label: A
options.text: Their cosine similarity is 1 because c points in the same direction as a, even though their Euclidean distance is 3

options.label: B
options.text: Their cosine similarity is 0.5 because c is twice as long

options.label: C
options.text: Their Euclidean distance is 0 because they point the same way

options.label: D
options.text: Their dot product is 9

stem: Which training objective is typically used for sentence-embedding models that power semantic search?
explanation: Contrastive training directly optimises the geometry search needs: queries land near the passages that answer them, even with few shared words.

options.label: A
options.text: Predicting only the next token

options.label: B
options.text: Minimising the squared difference between sentence lengths

options.label: C
options.text: Classifying every sentence into a fixed list of topics

options.label: D
options.text: A contrastive objective that pulls matching pairs (such as a question and its answering passage) together and pushes non-matching pairs apart

stem: What is cosine similarity, and why is it often preferred over the raw dot product for comparing embeddings?
explanation: Cosine compares direction only, so vector length does not distort rankings.

criteria.description: Defines cosine similarity as the dot product divided by the product of the vector lengths (or the cosine of the angle between them)
Explains that it ignores vector length/magnitude, so long vectors do not win just by being long
Adds a correct detail: range −1 to 1, or that for unit-normalised vectors it equals the dot product

rubric.modelAnswer: Cosine similarity is a·b / (‖a‖‖b‖), the cosine of the angle between the vectors, ranging from −1 to 1. It measures direction only, so a vector does not score highly just because it is long; the raw dot product grows with length and can rank a long but less related vector above a closer match. If embeddings are normalised to unit length, the dot product and cosine are identical, which is why many systems normalise once and then use the dot product.

stem: What does an attention layer output for each query?
explanation: Attention is a soft lookup: every value contributes in proportion to its weight. It only behaves like picking one item when the softmax saturates.

options.label: A
options.text: The single value whose key has the highest score

options.label: B

stem: Why does scaled dot-product attention divide the scores by √d_k?
explanation: With unit-variance entries, q·k has variance d_k. Unscaled, the softmax becomes nearly one-hot and its gradients vanish. Dividing by √d_k restores unit variance. The softmax already makes the weights sum to one, so that is not the reason.

options.label: A
options.text: Dot products grow with dimension (variance d_k), and large scores saturate the softmax towards one-hot, making gradients tiny

options.label: B

stem: Query and key entries are independent with mean 0 and variance 1. What is the variance of q·k when d_k = 64?
explanation: Each term q_i·k_i has variance 1, and the variances of 64 independent terms add to 64. The standard deviation is √64 = 8, which is why we divide by 8.

stem: In self-attention, where do the queries, keys and values come from?
explanation: Q = XW_Q, K = XW_K, V = XW_V: one input sequence, three learned projections. In cross-attention, by contrast, the keys and values come from a different sequence.

stem: How should a causal mask be applied in attention?
explanation: Adding −∞ before the softmax gives e^(−∞) = 0 and keeps each row summing to one. Zeroing weights after the softmax breaks that sum, and multiplying a score by zero gives a score of 0, which still receives positive weight.

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Multiply the scores of future positions by zero

options.label: D

options.label: C

stem: Explain why scaled dot-product attention divides the query–key scores by √d_k.
explanation: Dot-product variance grows with d_k; large scores saturate softmax and shrink gradients; scaling restores unit variance.

criteria.description: States that dot-product scores grow with dimension: with unit-variance entries the variance is d_k (standard deviation √d_k)
Explains that large scores push the softmax towards a one-hot (saturated) distribution
Explains that a saturated softmax has tiny gradients, so attention learns slowly or not at all
States that dividing by √d_k brings the score variance back to about 1, independent of dimension

rubric.modelAnswer: If query and key entries have mean 0 and variance 1, the dot product sums d_k terms of variance 1, so its variance is d_k and its typical size is √d_k (8 for d_k = 64). Softmax depends exponentially on score differences, so such large scores make it nearly one-hot. In that saturated regime the softmax Jacobian α_i(δ_ij − α_j) is close to zero, so gradients into W_Q and W_K vanish and the model barely learns. Dividing by √d_k rescales the scores to unit variance at any dimension, keeping the softmax responsive and gradients healthy.

stem: With d_model = 512 and 8 attention heads, what is each head's dimension d_k?
explanation: d_k = d_model / h = 512 / 8 = 64, so each head scales its scores by √64 = 8.

stem: Why does a Transformer need positional information, and how does RoPE provide it?
explanation: Attention is order-blind; RoPE rotates queries and keys by position so scores depend on relative offset.

criteria.description: Explains that self-attention is permutation-equivariant / treats input as a set, so word order is invisible without positional information
States that RoPE rotates query and key vectors (pairs of dimensions) by angles proportional to position
Explains that the query–key dot product then depends on the relative offset between positions

rubric.modelAnswer: Self-attention compares every token with every other token regardless of where they are, so permuting the input only permutes the output; without positional information 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' look identical. RoPE rotates each 2-D pair of dimensions in the query and key vectors by an angle proportional to the token's position. A query at position m and a key at position n then differ in angle by (m − n)θ, so their score depends on the relative distance, not the absolute positions.

explanation: Small chunks lose context; large chunks dilute embeddings and waste context; tune on an evaluation set.

criteria.description: Explains that chunks that are too small lose context (e.g. unresolved references) and more of them are needed
Explains that chunks that are too large have diluted embeddings that rank poorly and consume the context window
Suggests a sound way to handle it: test a few sizes on an evaluation set, use overlap, or use structure-aware or parent–child chunking

rubric.modelAnswer: Small chunks are precise but lose context: a sentence like 'it is divided by √d_k' is useless without saying what 'it' is, and answers need many chunks. Large chunks contain more context but their single embedding averages many topics, so they match specific queries poorly and use up the context window. A typical starting point is a few hundred tokens with 10–20% overlap, split along headings, then measured on real questions; parent–child retrieval can combine precise matching with fuller context.

stem: Explain how an HNSW index finds nearest neighbours quickly.
explanation: Greedy search on a layered proximity graph, from sparse top layers down to layer 0; approximate, tuned by ef_search.

criteria.description: Describes a graph in which each vector is linked to near neighbours and search greedily moves to the neighbour closest to the query
Describes the hierarchy: sparse upper layers with long hops, descending layer by layer to the full bottom layer
Notes that it is approximate, with a recall–latency trade-off controlled by parameters such as ef_search or M

rubric.modelAnswer: HNSW builds a graph where each vector links to some of its nearest neighbours. Searching means greedily walking from an entry point to whichever neighbour is closer to the query until no neighbour is closer. The graph has layers: every vector is in layer 0, and exponentially fewer appear in each higher layer, so the top layers act like express routes with long hops. Search starts at the top, descends to the closest node, drops a layer and repeats, then does a careful search in layer 0. It is approximate: raising ef_search (or M) increases recall at the cost of latency or memory.

criteria.description: Distinguishes the two: grounded means every claim is supported by the retrieved passages; an answer can be correct but ungrounded (from model memory) or grounded in a wrong source
States that every cited ID must be one of the passages actually retrieved/shown to the model
States that the cited passage must actually support the claim it is attached to

rubric.modelAnswer: A correct answer is factually right; a grounded answer is one whose every claim is supported by the passages the system retrieved. They differ: the model can give a correct answer from its own memory that no passage supports, which cannot be cited or verified. To check citations, first confirm that every cited ID is in the set of passages that were actually shown to the model (anything else is fabricated and should be stripped or flagged), then check that each cited passage really supports the sentence it is attached to, by rule-based checks or a calibrated judge.
